extracted.intended_audience: current and prospective peer reviewers for The BMJ (clinician and patient reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing peer review for manuscripts submitted to The BMJ, including the journal's open peer review policy, expectations about content and priorities, declarations of interests, and procedural steps for responding to review invitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign reports and declare competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: We ask reviewers to sign their reports and declare any competing interests on any manuscripts we send them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should explicitly sign their reports and disclose competing interests when reviewing for The BMJ. Reviews are advisory to editors, who make the final decision. Declared interests become part of the transparent record associated with the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review for research and analysis articles
rubrics_metrics.description: For research papers (from Sep 2014) and analysis articles (from Feb 2016) every accepted paper will have its prepublication history posted alongside it on thebmj.com.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prepublication history comprises all previous versions of the manuscript, the study protocol for research papers, the report from the manuscript committee meeting, the reviewers’ signed comments, and the authors’ responses. Reviewers should be aware their signed comments may be published and that the process is transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission of study protocol (mandatory for clinical trials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting the protocol is mandatory for all clinical trials and encouraged for all other studies at The BMJ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing research, expect the protocol to be available for clinical trials and often for other studies; use the protocol to check pre-specified methods and outcomes and assess deviations, selective reporting, and methodological rigour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help prioritise manuscripts by BMJ aims (original, important, reliable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to help prioritise manuscripts bearing in mind that The BMJ aims to publish original, important, and reliable articles that will help readers (mainly doctors) make better decisions about practice, policy, education, and research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising a manuscript, evaluate its originality, importance to the field, methodological reliability, and practical usefulness for clinical practice, policy, education, or future research. Use these priorities to inform your recommendation and comments to editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive critique that helps assess importance and originality
rubrics_metrics.description: For the best reviews (those that constructively critique the article and help editors assess its importance and originality) The BMJ offers up to 3 AMA PRA Category 1 CME points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce reviews that are constructive, focused on improving the manuscript, and that explicitly address the article's importance and originality. Clear, actionable comments aid editors' decisions and may qualify as high-quality reviews for CME recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient reviewers to judge importance and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to peer review, we also ask patient reviewers for their opinion on the importance and relevance of selected manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When patient reviewers are engaged, their role is specifically to comment on the importance and relevance of the work from a patient or public perspective. Reviewers should respect and incorporate patient input where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to review invitations via online editorial office
rubrics_metrics.description: If we need your help with appraising a manuscript we will email you and ask you to accept or reject the reviewing invitation at our online editorial office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely acceptance or declination of review invitations is expected. Use the online editorial office to respond. Prompt responses help the journal manage peer review workload and keep decisions timely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviews are advisory; editors make final decisions (possible manuscript committee meeting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers advise the editors, who make the final decision (aided by an editorial manuscript committee meeting for some articles, including original research).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame recommendations and critiques to assist editorial decision-making. Be aware that some manuscripts may be discussed in manuscript committee meetings and that editors retain ultimate responsibility for acceptance/rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review reports may be shared within BMJ journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can nominate other BMJ Journals that they would like their manuscript to go to automatically if it is rejected by the first journal. The system also passes on editors' comments and peer reviewers' reports relating to that manuscript, to facilitate the review process at the next BMJ journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should understand that their reports and editors' comments can be forwarded to other BMJ journals and seen by other editors, so write with the possibility of reuse in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers can access each other's reports after decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts sent for review are usually seen by at least two reviewers, and reviewers can access each other's reports on the same manuscript once The BMJ has made its decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This post-decision access is intended to provide useful feedback and learning. Write reports with clarity and professionalism as they may be viewed by co-reviewers later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and report ethical concerns (plagiarism, duplicate publication, fraud)
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ transparency policy pulls together advice on what to do if you are concerned about the ethics aspects of a manuscript, or if you suspect plagiarism, duplicate publication, or scientific fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you suspect ethical problems, follow The BMJ's transparency policy and guidance. Report concerns clearly to the editors rather than attempting to investigate independently; use provided contacts (eg, papersadmin@bmj.com) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of provenance on published articles
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of every accepted editorial, research article, clinical review, practice article, analysis article, feature, and head-to-head article The BMJ will add a statement explaining the article's provenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible provenance statements include: 'Not commissioned; externally peer reviewed', 'Not commissioned; not externally peer reviewed', 'Commissioned; externally peer reviewed', 'Commissioned; not externally peer reviewed', 'Commissioned, based on an idea from the author; externally peer reviewed', and 'Commissioned, based on an idea from the author; not externally peer reviewed'. Reviewers should be aware that provenance status will be declared on publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report adverse effects or concerns about open peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: If you experience any adverse event arising from open peer review, or would like to tell us your views, please email papersadmin@bmj.com.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open peer review has potential consequences; reviewers should notify the editorial office of any adverse experiences or concerns about the open process so the journal can respond.
